title: TB VFind: Using Data to Find Tuberculosis Before It Spreads
text:
Programme TB VFind, part of the “Dusit Model” for ending TB in the community


My role Chief of Innovation: designed the data collection, the dashboard and the tracking workflow


Where Vajira Hospital and communities in Dusit and neighbouring Bangkok districts


Partners Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA) health department and health centres; Fujifilm Thailand (portable X-ray)


Users The hospital TB clinic and public health nurses


Tools Google Forms, Google Sheets, a BI dashboard, ICD-10 coding, R for analysis

title: TB VFind: Using Data to Find Tuberculosis Before It Spreads
text:
Why it matters
Tuberculosis is curable, but it still spreads quietly in Bangkok. Bangkok reports more TB cases than any other province in Thailand, and many people carry the disease for months before they feel sick enough to see a doctor. By then, they may have passed it on to their family, neighbours and co-workers.
Waiting for patients to walk into a clinic finds TB late. Active case finding turns that around: the health team goes to the people most at risk, screens them with a chest X-ray and starts care early. The hard part is knowing where to go. That is a data problem, and it’s the part I worked on.

title: TB VFind: Using Data to Find Tuberculosis Before It Spreads
section: Using hospital data to decide where to screen
text:
Using hospital data to decide where to screen
Every new TB patient at Vajira Hospital already has an address in the hospital record. On its own that’s just a field in a form. Put together, every three months, it becomes a map of where TB is active right now.


The TB VFind loop: collect new TB cases, map hotspots, screen with BMA teams, refer and track, then collect again






Every
3 months
1 · Collectnew TB cases and addresses
2 · Maphotspots on the dashboard
3 · Screenwith BMA teams, on site
4 · Refer, trackto the nearest BMA service



Collect. Every three months, we pull the new TB cases from the hospital record, with the district and street of each patient’s home.
Map. The BI dashboard shows where new cases are clustering. Those hotspots are where the next round of screening goes.
Screen. Together with BMA public health teams, we go to the hotspot communities with a portable X-ray machine. Each person answers a short, structured set of risk questions and has a chest X-ray on the spot.
Refer and track. Anyone with suspected TB is referred to a named service, usually the BMA health centre or hospital closest to home, and the team follows them up there.

Then the loop starts again with fresh data, so the screening keeps moving to where it is needed most.

title: TB VFind: Using Data to Find Tuberculosis Before It Spreads
section: Turning free text into data we can use
text:
Turning free text into data we can use
Before TB VFind, TB history was written as free text in the hospital information system. It was readable by a doctor, but impossible to count, compare or map. I redesigned the collection so each answer became a structured field from the start.


1 Structured form. A TB VFind form in Google Forms replaces free-text notes: contact history, risk groups, symptoms, smoking, chronic disease, X-ray result.


2 One shared sheet. Answers land in Google Sheets, where ICD-10 codes, risk group and incidence are calculated automatically.


3 Live dashboard. A BI dashboard shows X-ray results, risk groups, referrals and hotspots, filtered by date, district and insurance scheme.


4 Shared with partners. Clean, coded data can be shared with BMA services and exported for the national TB programme, instead of re-typed.


With the data structured and coded from the start, our team found the whole process about twice as fast: no re-typing, no manual counting, and the dashboard updates itself.




The screening dashboard: chest X-ray results, X-ray findings among the abnormal films, and where each person was referred.





The risk dashboard: insurance scheme, sex, contact type, TB risk groups, metabolic risk, symptoms and smoking history.



Both screenshots are from August 2024, part-way through the first year. Patient lists and the case map are left out to protect privacy.

title: TB VFind: Using Data to Find Tuberculosis Before It Spreads
section: Working as one team across Bangkok
text:
Working as one team across Bangkok
TB doesn’t stop at a hospital’s front door, so neither could the project. It only works because people inside and outside the hospital share the same data and the same goal.


Inside Vajira Hospital

Pulmonary medicine and the TB clinic: clinical lead and diagnosis
Vajira Wisdom Centre: the BI dashboard
The ARI clinic: further tests for people referred to the hospital



Bangkok Metropolitan Administration

BMA health department: planning where and when to screen
BMA public health centres and their nurses: community screening and follow-up close to home
BMA hospitals, such as Klang Hospital: further tests and care



Outside partners

Fujifilm Thailand: the portable X-ray system used in the community (news release, March 2024)
National TB programme: case reporting and standards



The referral is the key moment. Every one of the 101 people with suspected TB was referred to a named service: 76 to BMA health centres and other public health services near home, and 25 to Vajira Hospital’s ARI clinic. Because the BMA network covers primary care across the city, patients can be followed up where they live, which is what keeps them on treatment.

Between March 2024 and July 2026, the teams screened 1,978 people. One in eight had an abnormal chest X-ray, and 101 people, about 1 in 20 of everyone screened, had an X-ray that looked like TB.

This is the strongest case for going out to find TB. 57 of the 101 people with suspected TB had no symptoms. If we had only screened people who said they had a cough, more than half of them would have been missed, and they would have kept living, working and sharing rooms with others without knowing.

Over three rounds of the loop, the share of people with suspected TB fell from 6.2% of those screened in 2024 to 5.1% in 2025 and 2.5% in the first seven months of 2026. This is what we hoped to see as cases in the hotspots are found and treated. It isn’t proof on its own: the communities screened change from round to round, and 2026 is a part year. That is why the next step is better, standardised data.
Of the 19 suspected cases with a final diagnosis recorded back in our sheet so far, 8 were confirmed active TB. The rest of the follow-up happens in BMA services, which is exactly why shared data matters.

title: TB VFind: Using Data to Find Tuberculosis Before It Spreads
text:
Why prevention is worth it
Finding one person with TB early protects more than one person. The WHO estimates that someone with untreated active TB can infect 10 to 15 other people in a year. Every early case stops a chain of new ones, and treating TB early is simpler, shorter and kinder than treating it late.
It pays off for the health system too. Japan is a good example. In 1955, TB took up 27.4% of the country’s medical spending. After decades of sustained TB control, it had fallen to 0.08% by 2011. Our team estimates that scaling a data-driven approach like TB VFind could save Thailand around ฿70 million a year in TB control costs. That is our projection, not a measured result.

Better quality of care


Timely
TB is found before symptoms start, in 56% of the suspected cases.


Equitable
Screening goes to crowded communities, migrants and people without insurance, who rarely come to a hospital first.


Patient-centred
X-rays happen in the community, and follow-up is at the health centre closest to home.


Effective
Hotspot data sends screening to the places with the most new cases.


Efficient
Structured data and automatic coding make reporting about twice as fast, with no re-typing.


Safe
Every suspected case has a named referral and is tracked, so fewer people are lost between services.

title: TB VFind: Using Data to Find Tuberculosis Before It Spreads
text:
What’s next

Data standardisation. Agree on shared data standards for TB tracking across hospitals and BMA services, so results can be compared fairly over time.
A custom application. Move from Google Workspace to a long-term, purpose-built system.
Wider collaboration. Work with digital-economy partners, including telecom companies, to reach more communities.
A health data centre. Lay the groundwork for a standardised health data centre that supports future research and ASEAN-wide collaboration.

TB VFind supports Thailand’s operational plan to end TB and the global goal to end the TB epidemic by 2030.

title: From Mid-Table to the Top 2%: My Competitions at Monash
text:
What changed: consistency
The two 2025 competitions came in Statistical Modelling, my first mathematics unit in a decade. I tried almost every method I had learned, and the results were average. Looking back, I had rushed past the most important part: exploring the data and understanding it before modelling. Tree-based models with pruning, such as XGBoost, were completely new to me.
So I changed how I work. Before each new competition I studied how experienced practitioners approached similar problems, on Kaggle, Medium, Reddit and other forums. I used AI coding assistants such as Claude to test ideas faster, and I kept looking for another way to improve the score after the obvious ones ran out.


3 semesters in a row with at least two competitions


6 of 6 results since 2026 ahead of at least 85% of the field


3 of 3 team competitions where the team used my model


That is the strength I’m proudest of: consistency. I don’t give up when a result is disappointing; I go back, learn what I missed and come again. This is only the first step of my machine learning career, and I’d love to work with people who bring the same energy.

title: From Mid-Table to the Top 2%: My Competitions at Monash
text:
Spotlight: forecasting Google’s stock price
My Applied Forecasting class ran a competition to forecast Google’s closing stock price on 5 October 2026. I made my forecast on 3 August, about two months ahead, and placed 5th out of 340.


US$345.00 my forecast, made on 3 August


US$343.83 actual closing price, 5 October


0.3% forecast error


I combined two technical-analysis tools: moving averages (MA), which smooth out day-to-day noise to show the trend, and the relative strength index (RSI), which shows when a stock has been bought or sold too heavily and is likely to turn.
A stock chart is more than a line. It records the greed and fear of millions of investors, and the uncertainty they live with. My result reflects that understanding of what sits behind the graph, not just the trend line. Health services face the same problem when they plan beds, staff and budgets under uncertainty, and that’s the kind of forecasting I want to bring to hospitals.

title: From Mid-Table to the Top 2%: My Competitions at Monash
text:
Insight
Eight competitions looked like eight different problems: stock prices, electricity demand, house prices, images, ICU patients. Underneath, every model had the same core. It learns patterns from past data, tests itself on data it hasn’t seen, and makes a prediction we can check. Change the data, and the same skills work in almost any sector.
That is what excites me about bringing machine learning back to medicine:

Predicting disease before it starts. The model that ranked ICU patients by risk of death can, with the right data, forecast who is likely to develop diabetes, heart disease or kidney failure, years before it happens. Health services could then step in with prevention instead of treatment.
Learning more from medical data. Models can find patterns across thousands of patients that no single doctor sees, giving us new insight into what drives disease and which care leads to the best outcome.
Genomic medicine. As genetic testing becomes routine, machine learning can help identify the people at high risk of cancer, so we can screen them earlier, or prevent the cancer altogether.
Beyond health care. The same tools can help with problems like global warming, for example searching plant data for species that absorb far more carbon dioxide than others.

The more good data we have, the more of these questions we can answer. That’s the work I want to do.

title: Scaling Health Check-ups With Data and Partners
text:
Programmes Off-site health check-ups for companies, and Vajira Hospital’s unit in Bangkok’s One Million free health check-up caravan


My role Project manager: workflow design, shared digital workspace, dashboard and partner coordination


Where Vajira Hospital Check Up Center, workplaces across Bangkok, and communities in the Dusit and District 4 zone


Partners Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA) Medical Service Department, Health Department and Dusit District Office; client companies


Built on Clinical decision support for check-up reports, LEAN patient flow, a BI dashboard


Years 2022 – 2025

title: Scaling Health Check-ups With Data and Partners
section: The idea: one system, two missions
text:
The idea: one system, two missions
Most chronic diseases, such as diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol, can be found years before they cause harm. A health check-up is the cheapest moment to catch them. The problem is scale: every check-up needs a doctor to read the results and write advice, and doctor time runs out long before demand does.
I managed two programmes that ran on the same answer to that problem.


Mission 1 · Business
Off-site check-ups for companies. The hospital takes its check-up service to the workplace. One agreement with a company brings in hundreds of employees at once, and the income helps the hospital fund its other services.


Mission 2 · Public health
Free check-ups for the community. Bangkok’s One Million Health Check-up campaign brings free screening to people who rarely see a doctor. Vajira Hospital ran a mobile unit as part of it, covering the Dusit and District 4 zone.


Both depended on the same three things: a fast, well-organised check-up day, reports that don’t wait for a doctor’s free hour, and partners who bring the people.

title: Scaling Health Check-ups With Data and Partners
text:
How the workflow fits together


1 Plan with the partner. A company’s HR team or a district office agrees the date, the place and who comes. Everyone shares one digital workspace, so the plan, the lists and the updates sit in one place.


2 Check-up day. A LEAN flow takes each person through registration, vital signs, blood tests and imaging in a fixed order, with no back-tracking and fewer queues.


3 Decision support drafts the report. Rules from Thai and international guidelines suggest the report and next steps. A doctor checks, edits and approves every one.


4 Results and follow-up. People get plain-language results with a clear next step. The dashboard shows the team how many were seen, what’s pending and what needs follow-up.


The decision support system is the engine. Without it, two doctors writing more than 60 reports a day by hand set the ceiling. With it, the same doctors approve drafted reports, and growth is limited by how many partners we can bring in, not by how fast we can type. The full story of that system is on the clinical decision support page.

section: Taking it to the community: the One Million campaign
text:
Taking it to the community: the One Million campaign
In December 2023 the BMA launched a campaign to give at least one million Bangkok residents a free health check-up, with hospitals, medical schools and district offices across all 50 districts (Nation Thailand). By March 2026 it had passed 1,002,629 people (BMA news).
Vajira Hospital joined with a mobile check-up caravan for the Dusit and District 4 zone. Our team brought the same workflow, the same digital workspace and the same report system that we had built for companies into the community. Our unit carried out around 33,000 check-ups, out of roughly 300,000 in the zone.
The kick-off, 23 December 2024. The caravan opened at the Army Transportation Officers’ Association in Dusit District, which offered the venue. The first people we screened were motorcycle taxi riders, who spend all day in traffic, strong sun and PM2.5 dust, together with staff of the Dusit District Office. It was a joint effort with the BMA Medical Service Department, the BMA Health Department and the Dusit District Office. Bangkok’s Deputy Governor, the Dusit District Director, and Vajira’s Dean and Hospital Director came to support the team on the day (Faculty of Medicine Vajira Hospital).




The caravan set up in the hall at the Army Transportation Officers’ Association, Dusit District.

title: Scaling Health Check-ups With Data and Partners
text:
Why it matters


Timely
Chronic disease is found at a check-up, years before it becomes a stroke or a heart attack.


Equitable
Free screening goes to motorcycle taxi riders and other workers who can’t easily take a day off to see a doctor.


Efficient
Doctors approve drafted reports instead of writing each one, so more people can be seen without more doctors.

title: Scaling Health Check-ups With Data and Partners
text:
Building something bigger
The check-up programmes, the TB VFind screening loop and the decision support system all point the same way: prevention works best when data, clinical rules and partners are joined up.

One record across services. Today a person may be screened by a caravan, a company check-up and a health centre, and each keeps its own record. Linking them would end repeated tests and show each person’s health over time.
Follow-up close to home. Abnormal results could go straight to the BMA health centre nearest the person’s home, the way TB VFind already refers suspected TB cases.
Population health insight. With consent and proper governance, the combined data could show each district’s health risks and guide where to screen next.
Longevity and precision prevention. The same model can grow into longevity check-ups, adding genetic and fitness testing.

The 33,000 figure is our unit’s total; the citywide total comes from the BMA.

title: Clinical Decision Support That Grew a Check-up Service 8×
text:
The opportunity
Demand for health check-ups was growing faster than doctors could keep up. Two doctors were each reporting more than 60 check-ups a day by hand: reading every lab result and writing every line of advice. Companies wanted to bring their whole workforce for check-ups, but doctor time capped how many the hospital could accept.
Patients had a problem too. Most health apps in Thailand simply flag results as normal or abnormal. A small, harmless abnormality shows up in red with no explanation, which can cause real anxiety, while the results that matter most don’t come with a clear next step.

title: Clinical Decision Support That Grew a Check-up Service 8×
text:
What we built
A decision support system behind the hospital’s patient app, Vajira at Home. It brings together everything from the check-up, applies the clinical guidelines, and drafts a personal report for the doctor to approve.


1 Collect. Lifestyle and history from the e-assessment, lab results from the lab system, and imaging.


2 Apply the guidelines. Rules from the Thai clinical practice guidelines and the ESC guidelines suggest the report and the next steps. Healthy results pass straight through.


3 Doctor approves. The suggestion appears on the doctor’s page. The doctor checks it, edits if needed and approves.


4 Patient reads it. The report arrives in the app with plain-language explanations of every result.



Three examples


Patient A
60 years old, smoker, long-term constipation.
Suggested
Colonoscopy screening, as the guideline recommends.


Patient B
30 years old, non-smoker, exercises fewer than 3 days a week, cholesterol 245 mg/dL, no medication.
Suggested
Lifestyle changes, and a repeat cholesterol test in 1 to 3 months.


Patient C
Same as patient B, but cholesterol 350 mg/dL.
Suggested
Start a statin alongside lifestyle changes.


Each suggestion goes to a doctor before the patient sees it. The system does the reading and the drafting; the doctor keeps the decision.

section: Growing the business without lowering the standard
text:
Growing the business without lowering the standard
Good data makes the service more precise for each patient and more valuable for the hospital at the same time. Every check-up feeds the next one.


The cycle of innovation: collect data, give precise reports, grow the business, support research, then collect better data






Cycle of
innovation
1 · Collectstructured data, every check-up
2 · Personaliseprecise, guideline-based reports
3 · Growmore companies, new services
4 · Researchbetter evidence, better rules



Collect. Every check-up adds structured lifestyle, lab and imaging data to the hospital record.
Personalise. The same data gives each patient a precise report and a clear next step, instead of a list of red flags.
Grow. Doctor time stops being the limit, so the hospital can take on more companies. The reports also point to services each person actually needs, such as vaccinations, exercise programmes, nutrition advice and follow-up by telemedicine.
Research. With consent and proper governance, the growing dataset supports future health research, which in turn improves the rules.


Quality and privacy safeguards

A doctor approves every report before the patient sees it.
The logic follows published guidelines: the Thai clinical practice guidelines, and the ESC guidelines for cardiovascular risk.
All data stays in the hospital information system, and a data sharing agreement and a data processing agreement are signed with every client company.

title: Clinical Decision Support That Grew a Check-up Service 8×
text:
What’s next

Longevity check-ups. Adding genetic testing and VO2max testing, so the same model can serve preventive and longevity medicine.
Rebuilding the logic as code. I designed the clinical content; I’m now rewriting the rules as tested, reproducible code so they can be updated and shared with other hospitals.
In the real world. The system supported the One Million Health Check-up Campaign in the Dusit and District 4 zone, around 33,000 free check-ups.

Bio
I’m a physician with five years of clinical and health-system experience in Thailand, now studying a Master of Health Data Analytics at Monash University on an Australia for ASEAN Scholarship.
My turn towards data came in 2021, as an intern in a rural hospital during COVID-19. Poor data systems slowed down care, wore out staff and contributed to deaths that could have been prevented. Since then I’ve worked on three things good data can do for a health system: make care safer, give staff their time back, and cut wasted cost, such as repeating blood tests and chest X-rays every time a patient is referred.
My focus now is health and business forecasting: using time series and machine learning to show health services what demand, risk and cost are about to look like.

title: Stopping Hepatitis B at Birth: An Award-Winning White Paper and Animation
text:
Event East Asian Medical Students’ Conference (EAMSC) 2018, AMSA International


Where and when Kathmandu, Nepal · January 2018


Topic Hepatitis B passed from mother to child in Thailand, and the role of vaccination


My role Initiator and team leader


Team Four medical students from Vajira


Result Winner, White Paper and Video Competition

title: Stopping Hepatitis B at Birth: An Award-Winning White Paper and Animation
text:
The theme: hepatitis B
Hepatitis B was the theme of EAMSC 2018. Within it, our team chose to focus on the route that matters most in Thailand: from mother to baby.
Hepatitis B is a virus that attacks the liver. In adults, most infections clear up. In newborns it’s the opposite: a baby infected at birth will very likely carry the virus for life, with a much higher risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer decades later. In countries like Thailand, the most common route has been from mother to baby around the time of birth.
That makes it one of the clearest cases for prevention in medicine. A vaccine given to the baby right after birth stops most of these infections, and Thailand has given hepatitis B vaccine to all newborns through its national immunisation programme for decades. But the protection isn’t perfect, and a small share of babies are still infected.

title: Stopping Hepatitis B at Birth: An Award-Winning White Paper and Animation
text:
What we did
Our team reviewed the published research to show how much Thailand’s hepatitis B vaccination scheme has reduced transmission from mother to child, and where the remaining gap lies. We turned the findings into two pieces:


White paper
A written review of the evidence on mother-to-child transmission in Thailand and on the impact of the national vaccination scheme.


Animated video
A three-minute animation that tells the same story to anyone, not just doctors: a mother, her newborn, a virus that wants to take over the baby’s liver, and the vaccine that stops it.



The video



Your browser can't play this video.

Our winning animation (3 minutes, on-screen text in English). The virus is a king trying to take the baby's liver castle. The doctor's vaccine defends it, but in about one baby in ten the vaccine alone isn't enough.

title: Stopping Hepatitis B at Birth: An Award-Winning White Paper and Animation
text:
Building the team
Nobody asked us to enter. I saw the competition, chose our angle on the theme and invited three classmates I knew would do excellent work. Then I split the work into two parts, reviewing and writing the evidence, and making the animation, and matched each person to the part they did best. My job was to keep the two halves telling one story and to deliver on time.
We had no funding. Everything came from our own time, between classes and exams.

title: Stopping Hepatitis B at Birth: An Award-Winning White Paper and Animation
text:
Presenting in Kathmandu

title: Data-Assisted Student Vaccination
text:
Years 2022 – 2024


My role Initiator and project manager


Where Vajira Hospital, Navamindradhiraj University (NMU), Bangkok


Team Student health check-up team


Tools UiPath · Google Sheets · Google Forms · SQL


Funding None. Self-initiated

title: Data-Assisted Student Vaccination
text:
The problem
Every year, new NMU students come to Vajira Hospital for a health check and vaccinations before they start. Healthcare students also need proof of immunity, so they are tested for hepatitis B and varicella (VZV IgG, HBsAg, anti-HBs).
Before this project, staff checked each student’s vaccine and lab history by eye in the hospital information system (HIS), and doctors keyed every vaccine order by hand. With around 1,200 students, the checks failed often. In the year before I started, some students received three or four doses of the same vaccine, and some had the same VZV IgG test three to five times in one year. Each repeat meant an unnecessary needle, a cost to the hospital, and staff time taken away from patients.

title: Data-Assisted Student Vaccination
text:
What I built
The aim was to give staff their time back: nurses back with patients, and doctors free to focus on the high-risk cases.

Pull the history from the record. I asked V-Wisdom, the hospital’s data team, to extract every student’s immunisation and lab history from the electronic medical record.
Sort students by risk. In Google Sheets I grouped students into healthcare and non-healthcare programmes, with subgroups based on their medical history.
Screen before the needle. I designed an online risk assessment in Google Forms that every student completes before receiving a vaccine.
Let a robot do the keying. I built a low-code UiPath robot that opens each visit and keys the lab and vaccine orders into the HIS. Clinicians reviewed every item before it went through.

title: Data-Assisted Student Vaccination
text:
Data and privacy

Sources: immunisation history and lab results from the hospital’s electronic medical record, extracted with SQL by the V-Wisdom data team.
Scale: about 1,200 students per intake.
Storage: kept only on the hospital’s own drive, and sensitive data was deleted at the end of every year.
Access: only the healthcare vaccination team could see it.
Safety check: every order the robot keyed was reviewed by a clinician.

title: Data-Assisted Student Vaccination
text:
Skills and technology







Tool
What I used it for




UiPath (low-code RPA)
Opening visits and keying lab and vaccine orders into the HIS


Google Forms
Online risk assessment before vaccination


Google Sheets
Grouping students by programme and medical history, and analysing lab results


SQL
Extracting immunisation and lab history from the medical record (with the data team)



UiPath was new to me on this project. The hardest part was teaching the robot to work precisely on the HIS screens, which were designed for people to click through by hand.
Then and now. I’d build it differently today. Instead of a robot clicking through screens, I’d connect to the hospital system through an API, keep the data in a proper database, and make the whole pipeline reproducible so another team could run it without me. I’d also design the safety checks into the system from the start.

title: Data-Assisted Student Vaccination
text:
Contribution to healthcare

Safe: every student is screened for risk before vaccination, and no student was harmed by an extra, unneeded dose.
Effective: students get the vaccines and tests their history says they need, and only those.
Patient-centred: the system uses data management to put each student’s safety first.
Timely: the whole intake is processed in two days instead of five.
Efficient: half the keying time per student, and no money spent on duplicate tests.
Equitable: every student goes through the same risk-based check.

title: Data-Assisted Student Vaccination
text:
What happened next
The project had no budget, so nobody took it over when I left for Monash in 2025, and the hospital went back to the old process. The hospital did let me trial something new, and I learned a lesson I still use: a project that depends on one person, or on spreadsheets that only one person understands, stops when that person leaves. That’s why reproducible data pipelines are now at the centre of how I work.
Where it could go. If hospitals coded their medicines with Thailand’s standard drug terminology (TMT), the risk grouping could run automatically across many hospitals and help prevent vaccine-preventable disease at a much larger scale.
